name: Golden Temple
info: The Golden Temple, or Harmandir Sahib, is the gurdwara at Amritsar in Punjab that Sikhs hold to be their holiest site, begun by Guru Arjan in 1581 around a pool dug by his predecessors and gilded under Ranjit Singh.

facts.made: Begun by Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, on a pool completed by Guru Ram Das; rebuilt by Sikhs after repeated destruction, and rebuilt in marble and copper by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who overlaid the sanctum with gold leaf
facts.form: A two-storey square sanctum, 12.25 by 12.25 metres, with a gold leaf dome, standing in a pool about 5.1 metres deep and reached by a causeway; a marble platform and a circumambulatory path 3.7 metres wide surround it, and four entrances open to the complex
facts.where: Amritsar, Punjab, India, in a complex that includes the Akal Takht, the offices of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, museums and a langar
facts.known: the sanctum in the Amrit Sarovar pool; the gold plating on the dome and upper level; the four entrances open to all; the Guru Granth Sahib installed within; the langar, a free vegetarian kitchen; the Akal Takht, the chief seat of authority in Sikhism; Operation Blue Star in 1984

t: Guru Arjan built the shrine lower than its surroundings and open on all sides, so that worshippers walk down to it, and on 16 August 1604 he placed a copy of the Adi Granth in it.
Mughal and Afghan forces attacked the site repeatedly, most severely in 1762, when Ahmad Shah Durrani had it blown up with gunpowder, and the Sikhs returned each time to restore the pool and rebuild.

In June 1984 the Indian Army's Operation Blue Star against Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and his followers in the complex damaged the shrine and destroyed the Akal Takht, and the casualty figures remain disputed.
dyk: Ranjit Singh's gilded copper panels for the roof were worth 500,000 rupees, and the first was placed on the shrine in 1803; the gold plating now includes a 400 kilogram dome and 750 kilograms of gold on the upper level.
ev: Guru Arjan began construction of the Harmandir Sahib, keeping the pool empty and dry while it was built
Guru Arjan placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the gurdwara and appointed Baba Buddha as the first granthi
Ahmad Shah Durrani had the Golden Temple blown up with gunpowder, and Jassa Singh Ahluwalia collected donations to rebuild it in 1764
Ranjit Singh donated gold to overlay the sanctum with gold leaf, after the renovation in marble and copper of 1809
Idols and images were removed from the Golden Temple after the campaign of the Tat Khalsa
The Indian Army carried out Operation Blue Star in the complex between 1 and 8 June, and the Akal Takht was destroyed
Sikhs rebuilt the Akal Takht Sahib, after repairs ordered in 1986 were removed

sections.origins:
The Golden Temple, also called the Harmandir Sahib or Durbar Sahib, stands in Amritsar, Punjab. Its early history is hard to reconstruct for lack of records: the few Persian sources tend to be biased, and most of what is known comes from Sikh hagiographical literature in the sakhi, mahima, gurbilas and panth prakash genres. These sources were written by poets rather than historians, are reverential toward the site and focus on theology more than on objective history.

Sikh sources hold that the site had long been associated with religion, fell into obscurity and was rediscovered by the Sikh gurus. Myths give it older antecedents, among them a Puranic-style account of an amrit kund, a reservoir of nectar, and a legend linked to the Ramayana in which Rama was healed by amrit brought by his sons Lava and Kush. According to Madanjit Kaur, the low-lying spot was probably a jungle with a pond and a Dukh Bhanjani Beri tree, near a caravan route. Sikh historical records say that Guru Amar Das chose the land, then called Guru Da Chakk, and asked his disciple Ram Das to find a place for a new town with a man-made pool at its centre. Ram Das succeeded him in 1574 and founded the town of Ramdaspur, completing the pool with the help of Baba Buddha and inviting merchants and artisans from other parts of India to settle there.
sections.content:
The Golden Temple is a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, set in a complex of buildings around the sanctum and the sarovar, the holy pool known as the Amrit Sarovar. The sanctum is a square of 12.25 by 12.25 metres with two storeys and a dome covered in gold leaf. It stands on a marble platform inside a nearly square pool of 154.5 by 148.5 metres and 5.1 metres deep, which a marble passage 3.7 metres wide encircles. Pilgrims usually walk clockwise round the pool before crossing the causeway to the sanctum through the Darshani Deorhi, a two-storey gateway that houses the temple offices and treasury.

The Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, is seated on the lower floor for about 20 hours each day. Each dawn it is carried in a flower-decorated palanquin across the causeway in the rite called prakash, and each night it returns to its bedroom in the Akal Takht in the rite called sukhasan. The interior carries mirror work, inlaid stone, embossed copper and murals, mostly of floral designs. The four entrances to the complex symbolise, in the Sikh view, that people of all groups, castes and ethnicities are welcome. Beside the shrine stand the Akal Takht, the langar, which serves a vegetarian meal to all visitors, and museums of Sikh history.
sections.making:
Guru Ram Das acquired the land, though two accounts exist of how: in one, taken from a Gazetteer record, Sikh donations of 700 rupees bought it from the people and owners of the village of Tung; in the other, Emperor Akbar donated it to Ram Das's wife. In 1581 Guru Arjan began construction, keeping the pool empty and dry throughout. The first version took eight years, and the brick gurdwara was complete in 1589. Arjan sited it below the level of the city to stress humility, left the compound open on all sides to show that it was open to all, and gave the sanctum a single bridge. Some later sources say that he invited the Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore to lay the foundation stone, a belief that is unsubstantiated; traditional Sikh sources such as the Sri Gur Suraj Parkash Granth say that Arjan laid it himself.

The pool was then filled, and on 16 August 1604 Arjan placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the gurdwara. Ranjit Singh took Amritsar in 1802 and announced that he would rebuild the shrine in marble and gold. The first gilded copper panel was placed in 1803, the temple was renovated in marble and copper in 1809, and in 1830 he donated gold to overlay the sanctum. Because so many people contributed, it is difficult to say when parts of the temple were built or decorated, or by whom.
sections.reception:
The completion of the first version was, in Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair's words, a milestone for Sikhism, since it gave the community a central pilgrimage place and rallying point set within a hub of trade. The canopy on the parkarma called Ath Sath Tirath, the shrine of 68 pilgrimages, reflects the belief that a visit to the temple equals visits to 68 Hindu pilgrimage sites. Bathing in the pool is believed by many Sikhs to have restorative powers. Sikhism officially admonishes pilgrimage, but an exception has been made for the Golden Temple, owing to the constant singing of hymns there. The Mughal rulers and Afghan sultans viewed it as the centre of the Sikh faith, and so as the main target of persecution.

Observers disagreed about its style. James Fergusson saw one of the forms into which Hindu temple architecture developed in the 19th century. A colonial list of 1875 claimed that Ranjit Singh's design was based on the shrine of the Sufi saint Mian Mir. Henry Hardy Cole took it to draw mainly on Islamic sources with significant Hindu input, and Percy Brown called it a synthesis of Islamic and Hindu styles with characteristics of its own. Hermann Goetz admired it but criticised its gaudy elements, and Ian Kerr and other scholars describe a mixture of Indo-Islamic Mughal and Hindu Rajput architecture. Louis E. Fenech finds the museum display partly ahistorical and typical of a presentation of Sikh history as persecution, martyrdom and bravery in war.
sections.survival:
The Mughal Empire arrested Guru Arjan, who refused to convert to Islam, and executed him in 1606. In 1709 the Sikhs defied an army sent to stop their festival gatherings, and in 1737 the Mughal governor of Lahore had the custodian Mani Singh executed; Masse Khan, appointed to police the temple, occupied it and befouled the pool, and Sikhs assassinated him there in August 1740. In 1746 Lakhpat Rai had the pool filled with sand, and the Sikhs restored it in 1749. In 1757 Ahmad Shah Durrani desecrated the temple, and in 1762 he had it blown up with gunpowder; Sikhs celebrated Diwali in its ruins. Jassa Singh Ahluwalia collected donations for its rebuilding in 1764, and on 1 December 1764 Baba Gurbaksh Singh and 29 other Sikhs were killed in a last stand against Afghan forces.

A new gateway, causeway and sanctum were completed in 1776 and the floor around the pool in 1784. The British built a Gothic clock tower beside the complex between 1862 and 1874, which the Sikhs disliked and demolished in the 1940s. No surviving account or depiction of the shrine before 1764 is known. Most of its murals were lost under later marble panels and in the demolition of the bungas, the buildings that surrounded it.
sections.legacy:
The Golden Temple became a centre of the Singh Sabha movement, which removed Brahmin priests, idols and images from it in 1905. After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919, in which 379 were killed, protests pressed the colonial government to transfer the temple's management to the elected Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, which still manages it. The complex was also the main centre of the Punjabi Suba movement, which led to the present borders of Punjab in 1966.

In the early 1980s Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and his followers took up residence in the complex. The government claimed that they made it an armoury and headquarters. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi ordered the army to remove them, and Operation Blue Star ran from 1 to 8 June 1984. Official estimates gave 83 army dead and 249 injured, 1,592 militants apprehended and 493 combined militant and civilian casualties, and the government attributed high civilian losses to militants using trapped pilgrims as human shields. The Associated Press correspondent Brahma Chellaney reported about 780 militants and civilians and 400 troops dead, and the government disputed his figures and charged him. Sikhs worldwide criticised the operation as an assault on their religion. On 31 October 1984 Gandhi was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards, and more than 3,000 Sikhs were killed in Delhi in the riots that followed. Volunteers renovated and drained the pool, and Sikhs rebuilt the Akal Takht in 1999.

summary: The Golden Temple at Amritsar, begun by Guru Arjan in 1581 and gilded under Ranjit Singh, is the holiest site of Sikhism. Mughal and Afghan armies destroyed it more than once and Sikhs rebuilt it; in 1984 Operation Blue Star damaged it and destroyed the Akal Takht.
references: Pardeep Singh Arshi, The Golden Temple: history, art, and architecture (Harman, 1989)
Louis E. Fenech, Historical Dictionary of Sikhism (Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, 2014)
Pashaura Singh, The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Jagjit Singh, Temple of Spirituality or Golden Temple, Amritsar (The Sikh Religious Tract Society, 1935)
notes: Start 1581 (Arjan began construction); the lead says the pool was completed by Ram Das in 1577 and the Amrit Sarovar section says Amar Das began digging in November 1573. Not used.
Bhindranwale's residence: the article gives July 1982 in one section and December 1983 in another; left out. Operation dates: 1-8 June in one place, fighting from 5 June in another; I give 1-8 June.

Casualties: official 493 combined militant and civilian casualties (History) vs official 492 civilians and 83 army (Operation Blue Star section) vs the lead's 'thousands' vs Chellaney's 780 and 400; I give the History section's official figures and Chellaney's, and not the lead.

The 1762 and 1764 destruction and rebuilding are told twice in the article with slightly different dates (rebuilt 1764, 1765 for the sanctum, 1776 for the gateway); I kept 1764 for the start of rebuilding and 1776/1784 for completion.
The article gives 'Jassa Singh' for rebuilding (Ahluwalia) and names Ramgarhia separately; not confused.
Left out: the ball-lightning legend of 1877, the 2021 and 2023 incidents, visitor numbers and UNESCO nomination, the lists of managers (empty).
'The article calls unsubstantiated' phrasing on Mian Mir should be reworded to 'a belief that is unsubstantiated' if the editor wishes.
